'''''Stevia rebaudiana''''' is a plant species in the genus ''[[Stevia (genus)|Stevia]]'' of the family [[Asteraceae]]. It is commonly known as '''candyleaf''', '''sweetleaf''' or '''sugarleaf'''.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=STRE2|taxon=Stevia rebaudiana|accessdate=3 December 2015}}</ref><ref name="mbg">{{cite web |title=''Stevia rebaudiana'' |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=e489 |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |accessdate=23 November 2019 |date=2019}}</ref>

It is a small seasonal plant which grows to a height of {{convert|30|-|60|cm|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}}.<ref name=mbg/> It has elongated leaves that grow along the stems and are lined up against each other. The flowers are typically trimmed to improve the taste of the leaves.<ref name="eb">{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/plant/stevia-plant|title=stevia {{!}} Description, Plant, & Sweetener|last=Petruzzello|first=Melissa|date=2017-12-12|website=Encyclopedia Britannica|publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica, inc.|language=en|access-date=2019-11-19}}</ref> Stevia is a tender perennial native to parts of [[Brazil]] and [[Paraguay]] having humid, wet environments.<ref name=mbg/><ref name=eb/>

Stevia is widely grown for its leaves, from which [[extract]]s can be manufactured as sweetener products known generically as [[stevia]] and sold under various trade names.<ref name="bi14">{{cite web |author1=Katie Jennings |title=Here's What The Stevia Sweetener Really Is – And Why Some People Think It Tastes Bad |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/what-is-stevia-why-does-it-taste-bad-2014-7 |publisher=Business Insider |accessdate=23 November 2019 |date=3 July 2014}}</ref> The chemical compounds that produce its sweetness are various [[steviol glycoside]]s (mainly [[stevioside]] and [[rebaudioside]]), which have 200–300 times the [[sweetness]] of sugar.<ref name=mbg/> Stevia leaves contain 9.1% stevioside and 3.8% [[rebaudioside A]].<ref name="pmid19961353">{{Cite journal |last1=Goyal |first1=S. K. |last2=Samsher |first2=null |last3=Goyal |first3=R. K. |date=February 2010 |title=Stevia (Stevia rebaudiana) a bio-sweetener: a review |journal=International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition |volume=61 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.3109/09637480903193049 |issn=1465-3478 |pmid=19961353 |s2cid=24564964}}</ref>[[File:Stevia-rebaudiana-total.JPG|thumb|right|upright|''Stevia rebaudiana'']]

==Description==
''Stevia rebaudiana'' is a perennial herb growing up to {{Convert|2|ft|m|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="mbg" /> The flowers are white with light purple accents and no fragrance. Plants produce fruit which is ribbed spindle-shaped. Stevia prefers sandy-like soil.<ref name=mbg/>

=== Chemistry ===
In 1931, chemists isolated the [[glycoside]]s stevioside and rebaudioside that give the leaves their sweet taste.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bridel |first=M. |author2=Lavielle, R. |year=1931 |title=Sur le principe sucre des feuilles de kaa-he-e (stevia rebaundiana B) |journal=Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences |issue=Parts 192 |pages=1123–5}}</ref> The exact structures of the [[aglycone]] [[steviol]] and its glycosides were published in 1955.{{scicn|date=May 2026}}

==Cultivation==
Beginning in the 1960s,<ref name=bi14/> commercial cultivation had spread to [[Japan]], [[Southeast Asia]] and the [[United States|US]], but also in mildly tropical climates in hilly areas of [[Nepal]] or India ([[Assam]] region). The plant prefers warm, moist and sunny conditions.<ref name=mbg/> The plant cannot survive frost during the winter and therefore [[greenhouse]]s are used to grow stevia in [[Europe]].<ref>{{Citation|last1=Ramesh|first1=K.|chapter=Cultivation of Stevia [Stevia rebaudiana (Bert.) Bertoni]: A Comprehensive Review|date=2006-01-01|volume=89|pages=137–177|publisher=Academic Press|doi=10.1016/s0065-2113(05)89003-0|last2=Singh|first2=Virendra|last3=Megeji|first3=Nima W.|title=Advances in Agronomy Volume 89|isbn=9780120008070}}</ref>

''Stevia rebaudiana'' is found in the wild in [[semiarid]] [[Habitat (ecology)|habitat]]s ranging from grassland to mountain terrain, does produce [[seed]]s, but only a small percentage of the seeds [[germinate]].

''Stevia rebaudiana'' has been grown on an experimental basis in [[Ontario]], Canada, since 1987 to determine the feasibility of commercial cultivation.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/crops/facts/stevia.htm |title=The Cultivation of Stevia, "Nature's Sweetener" |author=Todd J |year=2010 |publisher=Ontario Ministry of Agriculture and Food |accessdate=20 March 2014}}</ref> [[Duke University]] researchers developed a strategic plan to assist farmers and exporters [[Stevia cultivation in Paraguay|in Paraguay]] to compete in the global market for stevia.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cggc.duke.edu/pdfs/Duke_CGGC_Stevia_case_Paraguay.pdf |title=Strengthening the competitiveness of the stevia value chain in Paraguay |last1=Bamber |first1=P |last2=Fernandez-Stark |first2=K |year=2012 |publisher=Duke University Center on Globalization, Governance and Competitiveness |accessdate=20 March 2014 |archive-date=3 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303233837/http://www.cggc.duke.edu/pdfs/Duke_CGGC_Stevia_case_Paraguay.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Uses==
''Stevia rebaudiana'' has been used over centuries by the [[Guaraní people]] of Brazil and Paraguay, who called it ''ka'a he'ẽ'' ("sweet herb"), to sweeten the local [[yerba mate]] tea, as medicine, and as a "sweet treat".<ref name="Misra-2011">{{Cite journal |last1=Misra |first1=H. |last2=Soni |first2=M. |last3=Silawat |first3=N. |last4=Mehta |first4=D. |last5=Mehta |first5=B. K. |last6=Jain |first6=D. C. |date=Apr 2011 |title=Antidiabetic activity of medium-polar extract from the leaves of Stevia rebaudiana Bert. (Bertoni) on alloxan-induced diabetic rats |journal=J Pharm Bioallied Sci |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=242–8 |doi=10.4103/0975-7406.80779 |pmc=3103919 |pmid=21687353 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Rural and indigenous populations in Paraguay also used the plant as a contraceptive.<ref name="Schvartaman-1977">{{cite journal |last1=Schvartaman |first1=J. B. |last2=Krimer |first2=D. B. |last3=Azorero |first3=R. M. |date=1977 |title=Cytological effect of some medicinal plants used in the control of fertility |journal=Experientia |volume=33 |issue=5 |pages=663–665 |doi=10.1007/bf01946562 |pmid=862810 }}</ref><ref name="Planas-1968">{{cite journal |last1=Planas |first1=G. M. |last2=Kuć |first2=J. |date=1968 |title=Contraceptive Properties of Stevia rebaudiana |journal=Science |volume=162 |issue=3857 |pages=1007–1007 |doi=10.1126/science.162.3857.1007 |pmid=17744732 }}</ref>

In 1899, botanist [[Moisés Santiago Bertoni]] first described the plant as growing in eastern Paraguay, and observed its sweet taste.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Bertoni|first=Moisés Santiago|title=[no title cited]|journal=Revista de Agronomia de l'Assomption|volume=1|page=35|year=1899|lang=es}}</ref>

When extracts of its leaves are processed into a powder, stevia is used as a [[sugar substitute]] in most of the [[developed world]].<ref name="pmid19961353" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schiatti-Sisó |first1=Isabella Paola |last2=Quintana |first2=Somaris E. |last3=García-Zapateiro |first3=Luis Alberto |date=2022-03-02 |title=Stevia (Stevia rebaudiana) as a common sugar substitute and its application in food matrices: an updated review |journal=Journal of Food Science and Technology |volume=60 |issue=5 |pages=1483–1492 |doi=10.1007/s13197-022-05396-2 |issn=0022-1155 |pmc=10076456 |pmid=37033318}}</ref>

Based on the [[Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives|JECFA]] (Joint Expert Committee on Food Additives) declaration, safe consumption of [[steviol glycoside]]s for humans is determined to be 4 mg/kg body weight per day.<ref>{{Cite web |title=
STEVIOL GLYCOSIDES, Evaluations of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives |url=https://apps.who.int/food-additives-contaminants-jecfa-database/Home/Chemical/267 |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=apps.who.int}}</ref> It was also agreed by the [[European Commission]] in 2011 for use in food in European countries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=COMMISSION REGULATION (EU) No 1131/2011 |url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=OJ:L:2011:295:0205:0211:EN:PDF |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=eur-lex.europa.eu}}</ref> Steviol glycosides have also been accepted in the US as [[generally recognized as safe]] (GRAS).<ref>{{Cite web |title=GRN No. 278 Rebaudioside A purified from the leaves of Stevia rebaudiana (Bertoni) Bertoni |url=https://www.hfpappexternal.fda.gov/scripts/fdcc/index.cfm?set=grasnotices&id=278 |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=www.hfpappexternal.fda.gov}}</ref>

Stevia leaf and raw extracts are not treated as GRAS and their import into the US is not allowed for usage as sweeteners.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nutrition |first=Center for Food Safety and Applied |date=2019-02-09 |title=Additional Information about High-Intensity Sweeteners Permitted for Use in Food in the United States |url=https://www.fda.gov/food/food-additives-petitions/additional-information-about-high-intensity-sweeteners-permitted-use-food-united-states |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624234646/https://www.fda.gov/food/food-additives-petitions/additional-information-about-high-intensity-sweeteners-permitted-use-food-united-states |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 June 2019 |journal=FDA |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Import Alert 45–06 |url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_119.html |access-date=2019-11-23 |website=accessdata.fda.gov}}{{dead link|date=May 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>
